newsitem.title: USA: Fountains' Schlesinger, a Renaissance man.
newsitem.headline: Fountains' Schlesinger, a Renaissance man.

text.p: Adam Schlesinger of the critically acclaimed pop band "Fountains of Wayne" is something of a Renaissance man.

Not only did he write many of the songs, play numerous instruments and produce the oddly named band's debut album; he is also in another band called "Ivy" and is a partner in a recording company and an Academy Award nominee.

The first album from Schlesinger's "Fountains of Wayne," named after a shop in Wayne, New Jersey, that claims to have the largest selection of garden fountains anywhere, has been hailed as a masterpiece of infectiously catchy pop.

Schlesinger and fellow songwriter Chris Collingwood have been dubbed the new Leiber and Stoller -- the songwriters behind many of Elvis Presley's biggest hits -- or even the second coming of Lennon and McCartney.
"I'm certainly not going to complain if people want to say that," Schlesinger told Reuters.

He and Collingwood began playing together about a decade ago when they were at Williams College in Massachusetts. Originally they were called "The Wallflowers" but they sold that name to Jakob Dylan who has a band of the same name. After renaming themselves "Pin Wheel" they signed on with a small record label in 1992, but the company went out of business and their record was never released.

The duo then parted company. Schlesinger formed Ivy, which signed with Atlantic's Seed imprint, while Collingwood joined a country music band. When Collingwood moved to New York City in late 1995 they reunited.
20-30 SONGS IN A WEEK
"Within a week we had written 20 or 30 songs and we went in and put them on tape and that became the first half of our album," Schlesinger said. "We didn't labour over it too much."
The recordings, initially meant as a demo tape, produced some quirky humorous lyrics and memorable melodies.

"When we were younger we used to have our serious songs and our stupid songs, and the stupid songs were never performed for anyone and were really just to amuse ourselves," Schlesinger said. "The so-called serious songs were a little too earnest and adolescent and really trying too hard and somehow we found a way to lighten up a bit without making total novelty songs."

Lyrically the album has a light-hearted feel. Plenty of songs are about nothing in particular, like "Radiation Vibe," a sort of love song that Schlesinger said was written because "Chris just wanted to sing 'Baby, Baby, Baby.'"
Also behind the light-hearted feel to the album was the band's distaste for angst-ridden grunge music. "We've never thought of music as a way to express our inner turmoil," Schlesinger said.

Around the time the album was recorded, a friend, Jeremy Freeman, asked Schlesinger to become a partner in a new record label called Scratchie Records. Other partners in the company included Freeman's sister-in-law D'arcy Wretzky of the band Smashing Pumpkins and her bandmate James Iha. Fountains of Wayne became one of the first releases for the fledgling label and the Smashing Pumpkins connection was invaluable.
FROM ZERO TO 20,000
"We went from playing to zero people in October to over 20,000 a night with the Pumpkins two months later," Schlesinger said.

While touring to promote the album he was nominated for an Academy Award for writing the title song for "That Thing You Do" directed by Tom Hanks. "At that point things just became surreal. I never set out to be a film music person ... it was such a fluke and it kept escalating and escalating."
Stranger than being nominated was going to the Oscars.

"Surreal was the only word for it. You go and there's Barbra Streisand a row in front of you and there's Faye Dunaway right behind you and it seemed ludicrous for me to be sitting up there," Schlesinger said.

"I felt almost guilty about it. In a way I was actually upset that I didn't get nominated for a Grammy instead because going to the Grammys would have been so much more exciting," he said. "There is a lot of people in the music business that I'd love to get a chance to meet whereas I've never really wanted to meet a movie star."

Fountains of Wayne wrapped up a tour of the United States before taking off to conquer England, where their album was released last month. Later in the year Schlesinger will be back on the road with Ivy, who release their second album in the autumn.
If he can find the time he has other projects in mind as well. "I want to start the new Bananarama and ghostwrite the whole thing," he said. "You think I'm joking, but I'm not."
